extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars and policymakers in sociology/criminology interested in public discourse and ideologies of crime
extracted.subtask_description: Framework and typology for how explanations and lay ideologies of crime are constructed, deployed, and rooted in historical/theoretical traditions across judiciary, media, and public discourse.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal to 'common sense' as moral-political resource
rubrics_metrics.description: Reference to 'common sense' operates as a final moral appeal; it is harnessed to a traditionalist perspective on society, morality and the preservation of social order and forms the basis for constructing traditionalist coalitions and moral indignation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that common-sense appeals connect with 'Englishness' themes (work, discipline, the family) and draw out unarticulated anxieties among working-class sections; potency lies in themes/images rather than detailed specification of content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberal/cosmopolitan discourse's failure to connect
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'liberalism' of the cosmopolitan middle class has failed to touch deep roots of experience and is perceived as distant, academic and associated with 'permissiveness'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liberal positions on crime are argued in statistics, abstract analysis and quality newspapers and thus lack the pragmatic immediacy of traditionalist world-views in reaching working-class experience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explanations built from publicly available 'vocabularies of motive' (fragments/traces)
rubrics_metrics.description: Lay and public explanations draw piecemeal on social images, ideas of society and scattered meanings—'vocabularies of motive'—that are already objectivated in public language rather than produced afresh.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These explanatory elements are fragments of earlier coherent theories that have become sedimented in common sense (Gramsci's 'traces'); likened to Levi-Strauss's bricoleur assembling cultural oddments, e.g., religious 'traces' persist even in secular society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of explanation: to restore control and make events meaningful
rubrics_metrics.description: Providing an explanation for troubling events is a way to regain a sense of control; to give random/shocking events 'meaning' is to fold them back into a rational order that can be managed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explanations need not be logically coherent; their practical function is to render events intelligible and actionable rather than to satisfy strict logical protocols.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three main sites of explanatory production
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanations of crime arise primarily at three levels: in the judiciary, in the media (particularly feature articles), and among the ordinary lay public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each site has distinct character: judges provide condensed explanations tied to legal logic; the press probes backgrounds and causal models; the public uses available practical ideologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial explanations: condensed and limited (retribution, condemnation, deterrence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judicial discourse tends not to elaborate causal explanations; its primary tasks are retribution, condemnation and deterrence, and it draws from a very limited stock of explanatory models.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long theoretical disquisitions are unusual in court; judges operate under a 'logic' of judicial reasoning and precedent focused on plausibility rather than motivation—example: Lord Chief Justice Widgery's unease in the Handsworth case when motivations did not fit ready models.

rubrics_metrics.name: Press/feature articles: probe causes but within narrow constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Feature journalism attempts to explore backgrounds and causes of crime and thus furnishes more elaborated explanations than courts, but still operates within a limited range of paradigms and tight constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even supposedly 'environmental' explanations in the press are bounded by prevailing shared logics; the press's function encourages exploration but not wholesale theoretical innovation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited range of explanatory paradigms addressing shared questions
rubrics_metrics.description: A relatively narrow set of basic paradigms structures the variety of specific explanations; different positions (e.g., liberal and traditionalist) address the same core set of shared questions about crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These paradigms provide answers to common 'criminal questions'—such as motive, causation, and appropriate social responses—so debate is polarized around similar issues despite variant rhetoric.

rubrics_metrics.name: Central explanatory question: nature and responsibility of the criminal
rubrics_metrics.description: Explanatory frameworks hinge on what is attributed to the criminal—motivation, state of mind, degree of choice/responsibility—which in turn links to broader conceptions of human nature and relations between individual and society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Answers to this question determine views on penal objectives and punishment (e.g., punishment as retribution vs. rehabilitation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Typology of two basic lay ideologies: conservative/traditionalist vs liberal
rubrics_metrics.description: At the lay level two basic explanatory frameworks predominate and form a 'unity in difference'—a conservative/traditionalist schema and a liberal/social-schema—each assembling different answers to motive, nature, causation and response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are simplified caricatures used to show structuration of common attitudes; many diverse ideas fall under their shadows and variants exist within each.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservative (traditionalist) explanation of crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime is primitive, rooted in a moral struggle between Good and Evil; the criminal has chosen evil and is outside the human community and must be protected against; punishment severity scales with the crime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Has religious and secular variants (submission to God or social authority); emphasizes hierarchy and social order; criminal seen as threat to physical safety, moral duty and social code—punishment serves protection and warning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Liberal explanation of crime
rubrics_metrics.description: Crime stems from weakness, ignorance, poverty, poor socialization or social forces beyond the individual; it is a social problem amenable to remedy through socialisation, reform and support, although punishment and public safety still matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes psychologistic, reformist and deterministic variants; views individuals as vulnerable to larger forces and favors rehabilitative or remedial measures alongside necessary punitive responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical ideologies as 'assemblages' shaping everyday thinking and conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Common-sense structures are assemblages of maxims, morals, proverbs, beliefs and myths which supply institutionally appropriate rules of conduct and shape perception and behaviour—ideas become a 'material force'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These unsystematised, unfixed inner and outer speech patterns endow behaviour and conscious states with meaning and determine the horizons of what is knowable in society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical/theoretical roots leave 'traces' in common-sense explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: More articulated theories of crime (ancient divine law, classical liberalism, positivism, determinism) have left traces in common-sense ideas that resurface when lay thinking about crime activates these sleeping forms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include the divine/custom origins of early law, Beccaria's classical formulations, and later Benthamite/positivist contributions; such traces supply conceptual furniture for contemporary explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Neo-classical revision / positivist influence and the 'science of crime'
rubrics_metrics.description: Industrial capitalism and the growth of social science prompted a neo-classical revision in which forces shaping individuals (social conditions, classes) were emphasized and criminology as a 'science of crime' emerged using moral statistics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bentham advocated systematic study; the era saw biological/psychological positivism and sociological determinism influencing legal ideas and public discourse about crime.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of psychiatric and social-work professions in modifying law and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: Psychiatry and state social-work agencies acted as practical bearers of positivist/determinist ideologies, modifying notions of criminal responsibility and providing therapeutic/treatment alternatives within an interventionist welfare state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Both professions operate largely within an individualist determinism and case-work orientation (the so-called 'psychiatric deluge'), though social work is theoretically more ambiguous; they influenced policy-making and the humanitarian reform of institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class and political economy as generative context for crime theories
rubrics_metrics.description: Theories of crime and law are historically produced by the needs and positions of dominant and subordinate classes; legal forms and conceptions of crime help to perpetuate particular modes of production.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text stresses that theoretical positions are tied to social formations and class struggle rather than being neutral intellectual constructs (quoting Marx on law perpetuating modes of production).
